title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Car detailing
audience: Any home-service operator, including solo operators, starting or growing a business.
learningOutcomes: Write an offer with a clear promised outcome, time frame and conditions
Identify the friction and risk the customer carries and reduce them
Price the offer on value and cost, not only time

instruction.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer
instruction.body: "I will detail your car" is a service. "I will return your car on the agreed day with the exterior and interior done to the checklist on your work card, or I will redo any checklist item that fails at no charge" is an offer. The customer buys the finished car and the certainty that they will get it.

instruction.heading: The five parts of an offer
instruction.body: Set a clear outcome, such as a named package; a time frame, such as the agreed return day; the work the customer must do, such as booking a drop-off window and removing valuables; the certainty you give, such as a checklist and photos; and the risk you carry. Put the scope and exclusions in writing, because a written quote can become binding once it is accepted (business.gov.au, 1 August 2025).

instruction.heading: Packages instead of one rate
instruction.body: Car detailing is usually sold as packages. A Sydney vendor's list sets three tiers: Basic packages generally start around $120 to $180 depending on vehicle size, Mid-level packages usually sit between $170 and $400, and Premium packages start from $800 and can go past $1,000 depending on vehicle size and services (Schmicko, modified 8 August 2026). Those are advertised prices, not market data. A stepped structure, where each higher level adds something the customer can see, is one way to lay the tiers out (Jobber Academy, updated 8 October 2024), and Jobber lists car detailing among its examples.

instruction.heading: Reducing friction
instruction.body: Make the booking, the key handover and the return simple. Dealers can be a source of steady work: a consultant article reports that dealers may send business to a partner detail shop, including free washes for service customers, and describes dealer work as steadier than retail work. The same article gives no dealer rates or referral percentages (carwash.com, no date shown). Price dealer work from your own costs and hours, and put the dealer's terms in writing.

instruction.heading: Guarantees and claims
instruction.body: The Australian Consumer Law consumer guarantees apply to services. They require due care and skill, delivery within a reasonable time where none is agreed, and fitness for any stated purpose, and a business cannot remove them by contract or notice (ACCC, last modified 17 July 2026). A sealant or ceramic coating warranty is an extra promise that sits on top of those guarantees (business.gov.au, 27 May 2025). Any measured result, such as a percentage gain in gloss, must be substantiated before you publish it. The research found no verified product warranty or coating-specific rule, so check a coating supplier's terms yourself.

instruction.heading: Price the offer as one total
instruction.body: Show one total price that includes unavoidable fees. The ACCC's price display guidance (2 October 2026) says the total must include unavoidable fees, and that card surcharges cannot be charged from 1 October 2026. Price each package from the value the customer sees, then check it against cost and time before deciding on any premium.

procedure: Write the outcome of each package in one sentence a customer would repeat.
Set a time frame you have checked against your own completed jobs, and record how often you meet it.
List what the customer must do, such as the drop-off window and removing valuables, and reduce each step.
Add one certainty element to each package, such as a checklist and before-and-after photos, after checking the privacy steps in the safety section.
Decide the guarantee for each package and check that you can afford it.
Price each package from value, then check the rate against cost and time.

workedExamples.situation: A Sydney detailer offers a Basic package and a Mid-level package. Customers ask why the same package name costs different amounts on different cars. The sourced Basic range is $120 to $180 depending on vehicle size, and the sourced Mid-level range is $170 to $400 (Schmicko, a vendor source).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the rate card show so the price is clear before the car arrives?
workedExamples.reasoning: The rate card gives each package a vehicle size band, lists the steps included, such as wash, decontamination and sealant, and lists what is excluded, such as paint correction or heavy interior soiling. It shows one total including any unavoidable fee. The size band is what the sourced range depends on, so the customer can see why one car sits near the bottom of a range and another near the top.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only: a dealer offers to send each new car for a get-ready package and says it will send regular work. No dealer rate is sourced, and the research found no referral percentage.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the detailer price the dealer work from the retail Mid-level range of $170 to $400?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The retail range is advertised pricing for retail customers, and no dealer rate is sourced. The detailer prices the dealer work from their own costs and hours, and puts the dealer's terms in writing: the scope, the expected volume, any free washes for service customers and the payment terms. The detailer does not assume that dealer volume earns the retail rate.

equipmentAndPpe: Rate card with package names, vehicle size bands, included steps and exclusions
Checklist for each package, with space for photos and the client's sign-off
Written warranty template for any coating or sealant, kept separate from the consumer guarantees
Safety data sheet for every product used on the job (see the safety section)

commonErrors.error: Selling one hourly rate with no package scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Write each package with its steps, its vehicle size band and its exclusions.

commonErrors.error: Promising a paint or coating result you cannot show.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only results you have measured or can show, and state any warranty as an extra promise in writing.

commonErrors.error: Treating a warranty as a replacement for the consumer guarantees.
commonErrors.prevention: State that the consumer guarantees apply as well as any warranty you add.

commonErrors.error: Pricing dealer or fleet work from the retail range without evidence.
commonErrors.prevention: Price from your own costs and hours, and write the dealer or fleet terms down before any work starts. Gap: no dealer or fleet rate was sourced for this course.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Consumer guarantees for services apply under the Australian Consumer Law, and a business cannot exclude them by contract (ACCC, last modified 17 July 2026). Business guidance only: this lesson does not grant any licence or authority.
Show one total price including unavoidable fees, and say whether it includes GST, before you publish a price (ACCC, 2 October 2026). Check any surcharge rule against the ACCC page before you use it.

qualityStandard: Offer and pricing decisions are written down and checked against cost and time.
documentationEvidence: Written offer or plan, evidence collected, and the decision made.
summary: A detailing offer sells a finished car and a clear package, not an hourly rate.
Package prices depend on vehicle size, so state the size band and included steps on every rate card.
Gap: dealer, insurer and fleet channels are not verified for car detailing, and no dealer rate was sourced.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the customer buy in a car detailing offer?
options: The finished car, with a clear checklist and certainty
The number of polishing machines you own

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a package rate card state the vehicle size band?
options: Because the sourced package ranges depend on vehicle size
Because vehicle size has no effect on the work
Because customers prefer larger numbers on a page
Because it replaces the exclusions list

knowledgeChecks.question: A dealer offers regular work. What should set the price for that work?
options: The top of the retail Premium range, automatically
Your own costs and hours, with the dealer's terms in writing
The rate a dealer quotes on its website
Whatever the dealer offers, with no written terms

officialReferences.title: What the ACCC does: consumer rights and guarantees (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: States that services must be provided with due care and skill, within a reasonable time where no time is agreed, and fit for any stated purpose, and that businesses cannot remove these rights by contract or notice. Publisher: ACCC.

officialReferences.title: Price displays (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: States that the total price must include unavoidable fees, shown as a single figure, and that card surcharges cannot be charged from 1 October 2026. Publisher: ACCC.
